680.title: The Nativity of Mary (8 September)
680.hook: nine months after the Immaculate Conception, a birthday for Mary
680.tomorrow: The Exaltation of the Cross (14 September)
680.howItsDone: Catholics keep the feast of the Nativity of the Blessed Virgin Mary on 8 September, nine months after the Immaculate Conception; the Gospel is Matthew's genealogy, and in places such as Malta and parts of Italy and India the day is marked with processions and festivals.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Assumption, Mary taken up. Your line was she went ahead.

Count back nine months from the eighth of September, and you land on the eighth of December: the Immaculate Conception, the feast of Mary's conception in her mother's womb. The Church's calendar does the arithmetic on purpose. So today is a birthday. In Malta it's a public holiday; in Italian towns and in parts of India there are processions and sweets. And the Gospel the Church reads for it is one that's easy to skip: the long list of names at the start of Matthew.
screen: `DECEMBER TO SEPTEMBER: NINE MONTHS.` → `A BIRTHDAY.` → `A LIST OF NAMES.`

segments.voice: Like her parents' names, Mary's birth isn't told in the Bible. The details again come from the Protoevangelium of James, and an old tradition places her birth in Jerusalem, near the pool of Bethesda, where a church of Saint Anne stands today. The feast began in the East, and Rome took it up later. So why read a genealogy on her birthday? Matthew counts it out as three sets of fourteen generations, from Abraham through David and the exile, and it's not all heroes: a man who helped sell his brother, a king who arranged a soldier's death, and women with complicated stories, Tamar, Rahab, Ruth, and the wife of Urias. Ordinary, mixed-up people, generation after generation. Then the list breaks its own pattern. Line after line, it's been so-and-so begot so-and-so. At the end, in the Douay-Rheims: "And Jacob begot Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ." The rhythm stops at her. Mary's birthday is the Church saying: here is where the long, crooked family line was heading. One ordinary-looking girl, born, tradition says, to an older couple, in a city full of pilgrims. Catholics greet her today, often with the angel's own words from Luke: "Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with thee: blessed art thou among women." There's no cake in the liturgy. But in some towns, there is cake.
screen: `NOT IN THE BIBLE; A TRADITION.` · `THREE SETS OF FOURTEEN.` · `NOT ALL HEROES.` · `THE RHYTHM STOPS AT HER.` · then, large: `OF WHOM WAS BORN JESUS, WHO IS CALLED CHRIST.`

segments.voice: Think about the people in the line that led to you: names you know, names you don't. If you pray, greet Mary the way Catholics do, Hail, full of grace, and wish her a happy birthday; it's a simple, almost childlike thing, and that's the point. If you don't pray, think of a birthday you've forgotten lately, and how you might honor it.
Nativitas Mariae. Latin for the birth of Mary, kept nine months after the Immaculate Conception, on the eighth of September. Today's word.

681.title: The Exaltation of the Cross (14 September)
681.hook: the cross found in Jerusalem, honored as a tree of life
681.howItsDone: Catholics celebrate the feast of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross on 14 September with red vestments and the Gloria; the Gospel is John 3:13–17, and some parishes hold a veneration of a relic or crucifix.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Nativity of Mary and a long list of names. Your line was her birthday.

The Bible begins in a garden with a tree in the middle of it, the tree of life, and ends in a city where the tree of life grows again, beside a river. In between, Christians say, there's a third tree: two beams of rough wood on a hill outside Jerusalem. Good Friday is the day the Church grieves at that tree. But there's a second day for the cross, in September, with no grief in it at all. The priest wears red, the Gloria is sung, and the Church calls the cross by a startling name.
screen: `A TREE IN THE GARDEN.` → `A TREE IN THE CITY.` → `A THIRD TREE ON A HILL.`

segments.voice: The story begins with Helena, the mother of the emperor Constantine. Tradition says that late in her life she traveled to Jerusalem, had the hill of Calvary excavated, and found the wood of the cross there. Historians can't confirm the details, and the Church tells it as tradition. Constantine built a great church over the site of the tomb and Calvary. Tradition keeps its dedication on the thirteenth of September; on the fourteenth, the cross was lifted up and shown to the people. That's what exaltation means: lifting high. Centuries later, the story goes, a Persian army carried the relic off and the emperor Heraclius brought it back, and that homecoming became part of the feast too. The Gospel for the day is John three, where Jesus compares himself to the bronze serpent Moses raised in the desert, which healed anyone who looked at it. In the Douay-Rheims: "as Moses lifted up the serpent in the desert, so must the Son of man be lifted up." The thing that should mean death is lifted up as healing. A Latin hymn by the poet Venantius Fortunatus, still sung on Good Friday, has the line "Crux fidelis, inter omnes arbor una nobilis": faithful cross, the one noble tree among all trees. In the hymn, the instrument of execution becomes the tree of life. That reversal is today's feast.

Then think of one thing in your life that once felt like a dead end and became a way through.

682.title: Our Lady of Sorrows (15 September)
682.hook: the day after the cross, his mother
682.howItsDone: Catholics keep the memorial of Our Lady of Sorrows on 15 September, the day after the Exaltation of the Cross; the Stabat Mater may be sung as an optional sequence, and some pray the chaplet of the Seven Sorrows.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Exaltation of the Cross, lifted high. Your line was the tree of life.

Anyone who has sat beside a hospital bed knows the feeling of being unable to do anything. You can't fix it. You can't take the pain. All you can do is not leave. Yesterday the Church lifted the cross high. Today, the very next day, it turns to the person standing at the foot of it. Not the soldiers, not the crowd. His mother. The feast is Our Lady of Sorrows, and its word opens a medieval poem.
screen: `BESIDE A HOSPITAL BED.` → `YESTERDAY THE CROSS.` → `TODAY, HIS MOTHER.`

segments.voice: John's Gospel gives the scene in one line, in the Douay-Rheims: "Now there stood by the cross of Jesus, his mother." She stood. The other Gospels say many watched from a distance. John puts her close enough to hear him, and from the cross Jesus gives her to the beloved disciple, and the disciple to her. In the 1200s someone wrote a Latin poem on that one verb: "Stabat Mater dolorosa, juxta crucem lacrimosa." The sorrowful mother stood, weeping, beside the cross. It's often credited to the Franciscan poet Jacopone da Todi, though nobody can be sure. Today it may be sung at Mass as a sequence, and many churches sing it between the Stations of the Cross. Composers from Palestrina to Pergolesi to Dvořák set it to music. The feast also gathers seven sorrows that Catholic devotion counts in Mary's life: Simeon's warning in the Temple; the flight into Egypt; losing the twelve-year-old Jesus for three days; meeting him on the way to the cross; standing at the cross; receiving his body; and the burial. Simeon's line is in Luke: "And thy own soul a sword shall pierce." In paintings, she's shown with seven swords in her heart. What the feast honors isn't a mother who understood everything or could change anything. It's a mother who stayed.

segments.voice: Think of a mother who is grieving: a child lost, sick, far away or estranged, a child in prison; maybe someone you know, maybe a face from the news. Picture her standing where she has to stand, and don't try to fix anything. If you pray, pray for her, or pray a Hail Mary for her; if you don't, simply stay with her in your mind.

683.title: Saint Francis (4 October)
683.hook: the day animals are brought to church for blessing
683.tomorrow: Our Lady of the Rosary (7 October)
683.howItsDone: Catholics keep the memorial of Saint Francis of Assisi on 4 October, and many parishes hold a blessing of animals on or near the day; Franciscans celebrate it as a solemnity.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Our Lady of Sorrows and the Stabat Mater. Your line was the mother stood.

On or near the fourth of October, parish parking lots fill up with dogs on leashes, cats in carriers, a hamster in a shoebox, sometimes a horse, a goat, a goldfish in a bowl, and now and then a very patient iguana. A priest walks down the line with holy water and blesses each one. It's noisy and a little chaotic, and people who haven't been to church in years show up. The man behind it all died centuries ago, and near the end of his life, nearly blind and in pain, he wrote a song.
screen: `DOGS, CATS, A GOLDFISH.` → `A BLESSING FOR EACH ONE.` → `A SONG FROM A SICKBED.`

segments.voice: Francis of Assisi was the son of a rich cloth merchant, and he wanted to be a knight. Instead, after illness and a stint as a prisoner of war, he gave it all up, stripping off even his clothes before the bishop and his father. He lived in poverty, rebuilding ruined churches, caring for lepers, preaching peace. Others came to share that life, and then more. The animal stories are famous: preaching to the birds, making peace with a wolf that terrified the town of Gubbio. Those come from collections written after his death, and people tell them as stories. But the song is his own. Sick and almost blind, staying at San Damiano, he wrote the Canticle of the Creatures, not in Latin but in the everyday Italian of Umbria. It begins Laudato si', mi' Signore, praised be you, my Lord, and praises God through creation, calling each part family: brother sun, who brings the day; sister moon and the stars; brother wind; sister water, useful and humble and precious and pure; brother fire; and our sister, mother earth. Near his death he added one more verse, for sister death. The idea is older than Francis. In the Book of Daniel, in the Catholic Bible, three young men in a furnace sing, in the Douay-Rheims: "All ye works of the Lord, bless the Lord." What Francis added was the family. Not resources, not scenery: kin. In 2015 a pope who took his name borrowed the first line for a letter on care for the earth.

segments.voice: If you have a pet, sit beside it and rest a hand on it; if not, watch a bird at the window, a dog across the street, even an ant on the sidewalk, or picture an animal you've loved. Watch it breathe, alive the way you are. If you pray, ask God to bless it; if you don't, wish it well, as kin.

Your line: brother sun. In Francis's song, even the sun is part of the family. Until tomorrow.

684.title: Our Lady of the Rosary (7 October)
684.hook: October is the month of the rosary
684.howItsDone: Catholics keep the memorial of Our Lady of the Rosary on 7 October and dedicate October to the rosary; many pray it daily that month, alone, as families, or in parish groups, meditating on the joyful, sorrowful, glorious and luminous mysteries.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Saint Francis and his song of the creatures. Your line was brother sun.

Look at the rearview mirror of a taxi in Manila or Mexico City, or in the coat pocket of an old man on a bus in Kraków, and there's a decent chance you'll find a string of beads with a small cross at the end. Some people pray on it every day. Some carry it and haven't prayed it in years. Some were handed one at a funeral and kept it in a drawer. On the seventh of October the Church keeps a feast in its name, and the whole month belongs to it.
screen: `BEADS ON A REARVIEW MIRROR.` → `IN A POCKET, IN A DRAWER.` → `A FEAST, AND A MONTH.`

segments.voice: Rosary comes from the Latin rosarium, a rose garden: in the Middle Ages, a garland of prayers was pictured as a crown of roses offered to Mary. The shape grew out of the psalms. Monks prayed all hundred and fifty; lay people who couldn't read began praying a hundred and fifty Hail Marys or Our Fathers instead, counted on beads or knots. It was sometimes called Mary's psalter. A popular story says Mary gave the rosary to Saint Dominic. Historians find it taking shape gradually over the centuries instead, and the Dominicans did a great deal to spread it. Then the feast. On the seventh of October, 1571, the fleet of the Holy League, an alliance Pope Pius V had helped build, met the Ottoman navy at Lepanto, off the coast of Greece. Pius had asked Christians to pray the rosary. When word came of the victory, he set up a feast of Our Lady of Victory; his successor renamed it Our Lady of the Rosary. In the 1880s Pope Leo XIII wrote letter after letter about the rosary and gave it the whole month of October. The prayer itself is simple: five decades, each an Our Father, ten Hail Marys and a Glory Be, while you think through a mystery from the lives of Jesus and Mary. Joyful, sorrowful, glorious, and in 2002 John Paul II added the luminous mysteries, from Jesus's public life. The beads keep count so the mind can go somewhere else: to Bethlehem, to the garden, to the empty tomb.
screen: `ROSARIUM: A ROSE GARDEN.` · `150 HAIL MARYS FOR 150 PSALMS.` · `LEPANTO, 7 OCTOBER 1571.` · `FIVE DECADES, FOUR SETS OF MYSTERIES.`

segments.voice: Hold beads if you have them, or use your ten fingers, and choose one scene: a birth in a stable, perhaps, or the empty tomb. If you pray, pray an Our Father and as many Hail Marys as you have time for, keeping the scene in mind; if you don't, move from finger to finger, one breath each, picturing it.

685.title: All Saints (1 November)
685.howItsDone: Catholics celebrate All Saints on 1 November as a solemnity and, in many countries, a holy day of obligation, with the Beatitudes as the Gospel; in some parishes children dress as saints the evening before.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Our Lady of the Rosary and a garden of prayers. Your line was the month of beads.

The Church's calendar is crowded with saints: apostles and martyrs, popes and peasants, page after page of names, each with a day. Yet behind those names, the Church believes, there's a crowd beyond counting. A farmer in a village nobody's heard of who prayed every morning of his life. A night nurse. A man who quietly forgave his brother. No statue, no day, no feast. So once a year the Church throws them all one party.
screen: `PAGE AFTER PAGE OF NAMES.` → `A CROWD BEYOND COUNTING.` → `ONE FEAST FOR ALL OF THEM.`

segments.voice: The feast grew from the martyrs. In the early centuries there were so many that no calendar could hold them, and Christians in the East began keeping one day for all martyrs together. In Rome, Pope Boniface IV took the Pantheon, the old temple to all the Roman gods, and dedicated it to Mary and all the martyrs. Later, Pope Gregory III dedicated a chapel at Saint Peter's to all the saints, and the first of November became the date, spreading across the West. The reading comes from Revelation, in the Douay-Rheims: "After this I saw a great multitude, which no man could number, of all nations, and tribes, and peoples, and tongues, standing before the throne." Which no man could number. That's the point. In Catholic teaching, a saint isn't only someone the Church has formally canonized. Canonization says, with confidence, this person is in heaven and can be held up as an example. But everyone in heaven is a saint, and the Church assumes that's a huge crowd, most of them never named. The Gospel is the Beatitudes: blessed are the poor in spirit, the meek, the merciful, the peacemakers. Not a list of famous deeds; a description of ordinary people living a certain way. All Saints is a solemnity and, in many countries, a holy day of obligation. And it opens a two-day pair: tomorrow, all who have died.

segments.voice: Let someone come to mind whose goodness nobody ever wrote down: a relative, a teacher, the woman who ran the parish soup kitchen, a neighbor who checked on everyone, living or dead. Picture their hands and what those hands did. If you pray, thank God for them, or ask their prayers, as Catholics do; if you don't, simply honor them in silence.
All Saints. The first of November, a feast for every saint in heaven, the known and the unknown, the multitude no one could number. Today's word.

686.title: All Souls (2 November)
686.hook: November is the month of the dead; graves visited and names read
686.tomorrow: The Dedication of the Lateran (9 November)
686.howItsDone: On All Souls Day, 2 November, Catholics pray for the dead, attend Mass, and visit and decorate graves; through November many parishes keep a book of names of the dead near the altar and read aloud the names of parishioners who died that year.

segments.voice: Yesterday, All Saints, the multitude no one could number. Your line was the ones nobody knew.

In the first days of November, the cemeteries of Poland glow after dark. Small candles in red and white glass jars flicker on grave after grave, the famous and the forgotten, until a whole hillside looks like a field of embers. In Mexico, families sit at graves with marigolds and food. In a parish church in Ohio, a priest stands at the ambo and reads aloud, one by one, the names of everyone from the parish who died in the past year.
screen: `CANDLES ON EVERY GRAVE.` → `MARIGOLDS AND FOOD.` → `THE NAMES READ ALOUD.`

segments.voice: Yesterday was for all the saints in heaven. Today is for all the faithful departed: everyone who has died, and especially those who, Catholics believe, are still being made ready for God. The Church calls that purification purgatory. It isn't a second chance or a halfway hell; it's understood as the last stretch of being healed, and Catholics believe the living can help with their prayers. One scripture the Church points to is in the second book of Maccabees, which is in the Catholic Bible. After a battle, Judas Maccabeus takes up a collection so that sacrifice can be offered for the fallen, and the text says, in the Douay-Rheims: "It is therefore a holy and wholesome thought to pray for the dead." Christians differ here. Catholics and Orthodox Christians pray for the dead; many Protestant churches do not, and Protestant Bibles leave Maccabees out or set it apart with the Apocrypha. As a single day, All Souls comes from a monastery. Odilo, abbot of the great monastery of Cluny in France, ordered his monks to pray for all the dead on the day after All Saints, and the custom spread. During the First World War, with so many dying, Pope Benedict XV allowed every priest to celebrate three Masses on this day. The old Latin prayer for the dead, still said at funerals and graves, is short: "Requiem aeternam dona eis, Domine." Eternal rest give unto them, O Lord. That's where the word requiem comes from. And week ninety-eight closes: Mary's birthday, the cross lifted high, the mother who stood, Francis, the rosary, all the saints, and now all the dead.
screen: `ALL THE FAITHFUL DEPARTED.` · `PURGATORY: THE LAST HEALING.` · `MACCABEES: PRAY FOR THE DEAD.` · `ODILO OF CLUNY: A DAY FOR ALL.` · then, large: `A HOLY AND WHOLESOME THOUGHT TO PRAY FOR THE DEAD.`

segments.voice: Stand at a grave you know, if there's a cemetery near you, or sit and bring one person who has died to mind. Say their full name, out loud if you can, and remember one specific thing: a voice, a phrase, a smell. If you pray, say the old line, eternal rest give unto them, O Lord; if you don't, simply remember.
All Souls. The second of November, when Catholics pray for all the faithful departed, and the beginning of the month of the dead. Today's word.
Your line: we remember. All through November, the Church keeps remembering too. That's day six hundred eighty-six.
